Worry
WUR-ee
adj./n. (from Old English wyrgan; anxious, distracted care about temporal things that displaces trust in God's sovereign provision)
From Old English wyrgan (to strangle, choke; said of a dog killing its prey by strangling), from Proto-Germanic *wurgjan. The image is visceral — worry as a strangling force that cuts off breath and peace. By extension the word came to mean anxious, consuming preoccupation. The Greek merimna / merimnao (used in Matthew 6:25–34) carries the sense of a divided, distracted mind — meros (part, division) + nous (mind): the worried person is the person whose mind has been split from its proper resting place in God.

Biblical Definition

Worry in the biblical account is not merely emotional discomfort but a theological disorder: the displacement of faith in God's sovereign provision by preoccupation with temporal contingencies. Jesus addresses it directly in Matthew 6:25–34, commanding “do not be anxious” (mē merimnate) three times and grounding the prohibition in the Father's care for His creation: the birds of the air are fed without sowing or reaping; the lilies of the field are clothed without labor — how much more will the heavenly Father provide for those He has made in His image? The argument is from the lesser to the greater: if God superintends His non-covenant creatures with providential care, His covenant children are infinitely more secure. Jesus identifies worry as the characteristic disposition of “the Gentiles” (Matthew 6:32) — those who have no covenant God and must scramble for themselves — and contrasts it with the kingdom-seeking that should govern the disciple: “But seek first His kingdom and His righteousness, and all these things shall be added to you” (6:33). Philippians 4:6 provides the positive command alongside the prohibition: “Be careful for nothing; but in every thing by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving let your requests be made known unto God.” The antidote to worry is not stoic self-control but specific, thankful prayer that returns the burden to the sovereign God who governs all things. Worry is thus the practical evidence of failing to trust the God who knows what His children need before they ask (Matthew 6:8).

Webster 1828 Definition

Worry (Greek merimna, divided mind) is the theological disorder of anxious, consuming preoccupation with temporal contingencies — the displacement of faith in God's sovereign provision by practical unbelief; forbidden by Christ in Matthew 6:25–34 and replaced by prayer and kingdom-seeking.

WORRY, v./n. [Old English wyrgan, to strangle.] To afflict with distressing uneasiness; to be anxious or solicitous about temporal contingencies. The root image is of being strangled — worry as a force that cuts off the ease and peace that trust in God should produce. In biblical usage, the Greek merimna (from meros, part; divided) names the anxious, distracted mind that has lost its resting place in God.

Jesus' threefold prohibition in Matthew 6:25–34 (“do not be anxious”) treats worry not as a personality type but as a sin — specifically the sin of practical unbelief in the Father's sovereign and attentive provision. The prohibition is commanded, not merely advised; its violation is addressed as a failure of faith, not a natural emotional limitation.

The two analogies (birds fed, lilies clothed, Matt. 6:26–30) employ the a fortiori argument: if God provides for non-covenant creatures that neither labor nor store, His covenant children under His particular care are infinitely more securely provided for. The argument is not “relax; things usually work out” but “the sovereign Father who sustains all creation governs your life; distrust of His governance is the root of your worry.”

The identification of worry with “the Gentiles” (Matthew 6:32) is theologically precise: those without covenant access to the God who knows and provides are correctly anxious by rational necessity. The Christian who worries is acting like one who has no Father — living as if the covenant were not real, as if prayer were ineffective, as if God did not know what His children needed.

Philippians 4:6–7 completes the biblical picture: “Be careful for nothing; but in every thing by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving let your requests be made known unto God. And the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, will guard your hearts and your minds in Christ Jesus.” The antidote is specific prayer, not general trust; the result is divine peace that cannot be manufactured by willpower but is given by the God to whom the worried soul has entrusted its burden.

Key Scripture

Matthew 6:25 — "Therefore I say unto you, Take no thought for your life, what ye shall eat, or what ye shall drink; nor yet for your body, what ye shall put on. Is not the life more than meat, and the body than raiment?"

Matthew 6:33 — "But seek ye first the kingdom of God, and his righteousness; and all these things shall be added unto you."

Matthew 6:34 — "Take therefore no thought for the morrow: for the morrow shall take thought for the things of itself. Sufficient unto the day is the evil thereof."

Philippians 4:6 — "Be careful for nothing; but in every thing by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving let your requests be made known unto God."

Modern Corruption

Therapeutic culture has reclassified worry as a medical condition (anxiety disorder) requiring pharmacological and psychological intervention rather than a theological disorder requiring repentance, prayer, and renewed trust in God's sovereign provision; while prosperity theology promises that obedient believers need never face the occasions of worry.

expand to see more

Modern psychology and psychiatry have reclassified worry-as-sin as anxiety-as-disorder, treating anxious preoccupation primarily as a neurological or environmental condition to be managed through medication, cognitive-behavioral therapy, and therapeutic self-work. This framework is not entirely wrong — genuine anxiety disorders with neurological components are real and deserve compassionate care — but it cannot remain the primary register for the pastor, because the New Testament treats ordinary worry as a theological failure, not a medical one. Jesus does not say “manage your anxiety through evidence-based techniques”; He says “do not be anxious” and grounds the command in the Father's covenant faithfulness. The therapeutic reclassification systematically replaces the call to faith with the call to technique.

Prosperity-gospel theology creates the opposite error: it promises that the truly believing, tithing, confessing Christian will be exempt from the circumstances that generate worry — guaranteed health, financial provision, and favorable outcomes. This eliminates the occasion of the Philippians 4:6 command by promising that obedient believers will not face situations that tempt to worry. Jesus, however, located His prohibition in the context of ordinary earthly life — food, drink, clothing, tomorrow — not in a circumstantially protected existence. The peace of God (Phil. 4:7) is promised to those who pray under pressure, not to those who have been shielded from pressure by divine favor.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

The biblical treatment of worry flows from the Psalter's cast-your-burden tradition (Psalm 55:22; 37:5), the Mosaic covenant's promise of divine provision (Deuteronomy 8:3), and the prophets' “fear not” commands to Israel in covenant relationship with the providing God.

expand to see more

Deuteronomy 8:3 (manna theology) — God fed Israel with manna to teach them that “man shall not live by bread alone but by every word that proceeds from the mouth of God”; the manna lesson is the Old Testament version of Matthew 6:25 — earthly provision comes from the word of God, not human industry alone.

Psalm 55:22 (casting the burden) — “Cast your burden upon the LORD and He will sustain you”; the Psalter's consistent direction of the anxious soul is not toward self-management but toward covenantal deposit of the burden with the God who will not allow the righteous to be shaken.

Isaiah 41:10 (“fear not, for I am with you”) — the “fear not” commands of Isaiah's latter chapters (chs. 40–55) address exiled Israel with the same logic Jesus uses in Matthew 6: the covenant-keeping God's presence is the ground for releasing anxious preoccupation with earthly contingency.

Matthew 6:25–34 (Jesus' threefold prohibition) — the command “do not be anxious” appears three times, each time grounded in a different argument: creation care (6:26), the uselessness of worry (6:27), lily-clothing (6:28–30), the Gentile alternative (6:32), and the kingdom-first command (6:33).

Philippians 4:6–7 (prayer-peace link) — Paul's command is the New Testament's most direct application of the Jesus tradition on worry: the antidote is specific, thankful prayer; the result is the peace of God that guards the heart and mind; the mechanism is entrusting the burden to the sovereign God.

Usage

"Jesus' identification of worry as “the Gentiles seek:)” (Matthew 6:32) is the sharpest pastoral rebuke: the Christian who worries is functionally living as if he had no covenant Father, as if prayer were ineffective, and as if the kingdom were not yet real — the pastoral call is not to calm the feelings but to renew the faith that generates peace."

"The Philippians 4:6 command to bring every worry to God in specific, thankful prayer is not a psychological technique but a theological discipline: it is the act of faith that hands the burden back to the sovereign God and receives, not the resolution of the circumstance, but the peace that surpasses understanding."

"Pastors who preach Matthew 6:25–34 must hold together the command (“do not be anxious” — this is a theological disorder) and the gospel ground (“your heavenly Father knows what you need” — this is a gospel promise): the command makes sense only as a call to renewed faith in the Father who governs all things for His children's good."
